lessons.title: Lesson 1: Setting a learning goal that leads to a job
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a learning goal connected to a real job.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job you want, you will write a learning goal connected to that job, in one sentence, with any licensing rules checked with the state board.
Learning is most useful when it leads somewhere. Start with the job you want, then work backward to what you need to learn.
Ask AI: "I want to work as a forklift operator or in a warehouse lead role. What training or certificates do people usually get for that? Which ones are short and low-cost?" Or: "I want to be an electrician. What are the usual steps?"
Some jobs need a license, and some licensing rules consider a person's record. Check with your state's licensing board or a reentry program before you invest time and money. AI can give you a starting list, but the official board has the final word.
Step by step:
- Name the job you want.
- Ask AI what training people usually get for it.
- Pick the shortest useful next step.
- If it needs a license, check your state licensing board.
- Write your goal in one sentence.
Words to know:
- Certificate: proof you finished a training program in a specific skill.
- High school equivalency: a test, such as the GED, that shows high school level skills.
Try it now: Write the job you want. Ask an AI assistant what training people usually get for it, and write your learning goal in one sentence.
You can now set a learning goal that leads to a job.

options: A college degree
Proof you finished training in a skill
A job offer
A loan
check.why: A certificate shows you finished training in a specific skill.

check.q: You want to become an electrician. How would you start your learning goal?
options: Sign up for the first class you see
Ask a friend which class is easiest
Start with the job, then find the training it needs and check the state licensing board
Wait until someone offers you training
check.why: Starting from the job and checking the licensing board leads to the right training.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Finding free and low-cost programs
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find at least two real programs that match your goal.
This lesson builds toward: Using careeronestop.org, libraries, adult schools or community colleges, you will find at least two real programs that match your goal, with phone numbers taken from their official sites.
There are many places to learn for little or no money: adult education centers (often for high school equivalency and English), public libraries, community colleges, reentry programs, and American Job Centers, which can offer career counseling and training referrals.
Find your nearest American Job Center with the CareerOneStop finder at careeronestop.org, a US Department of Labor site, or call its helpline at 1-877-872-5627. Services differ by center, so call or visit to confirm what yours offers.
Online, many respected sites offer free lessons, such as Khan Academy for math and reading and free courses from community colleges. Ask AI for ideas, then go to each program's own website to confirm it exists and what it costs.
Step by step:
- Ask AI where people in your area can learn your skill.
- Look up your nearest American Job Center on careeronestop.org.
- Check your library, adult school and community college.
- Write down two programs.
- Confirm each on its own website or by phone.
Words to know:
- American Job Center: a US Department of Labor-funded office that helps with jobs and training.
- Community college: a local, lower-cost college with certificates and two-year degrees.
Official sources:
- CareerOneStop: American Job Center Finder (US Department of Labor)
Try it now: Find your nearest American Job Center on careeronestop.org and one other program (library, adult school or community college) for your goal. Write down both, with phone numbers from their official sites.
You can now find free and low-cost programs for your learning goal.

options: A local, lower-cost college
An online-only school
A private job agency
A high school for adults only
check.why: Community colleges are local and usually cost less than other colleges.

check.q: AI suggests a training program near you. What would you do?
options: Sign up right away
Pay a deposit to hold a seat
Share it without checking
Confirm it on the program's own website
check.why: AI can be wrong, so you confirm programs on their official site.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Checking a program before you sign up
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask five questions to check whether a program is real and worth it.
This lesson builds toward: Given one program, you will check it with five questions on cost, length, schedule, what you earn and how it helps you get hired, with answers from the program itself and any pressure to sign a big loan treated as a red flag.
Some programs are excellent. Some cost a lot and lead nowhere, and a few are scams that target people who want a fresh start. Check before you sign or pay.
Ask five questions: What is the total cost, including books and fees? How long does it take, and what is the schedule? What do I earn at the end (a certificate, license or credits)? Is the school accredited or the certificate recognized by employers? How many graduates get jobs, and does it help with job placement?
AI can help you prepare the questions and explain words like "accredited". But the answers must come from the program itself, in writing, and from your own checks. Be wary of pressure to sign today or to take a big loan.
Step by step:
- Ask about total cost.
- Ask about length and schedule.
- Ask what you earn at the end.
- Ask if it is accredited or recognized by employers.
- Ask about job results and placement help.
Words to know:
- Accredited: approved by an official group that checks a school's quality.
- Job placement: help finding a job after you finish.
Try it now: Pick one program from Lesson 2. Ask an AI assistant to help you turn the five questions into a short phone script, then call or check the program's website and write down the answers.
You can now check a program with five questions before you sign up.

options: Approved by an official quality group
Free of charge
Online only
Run by the government
check.why: Accreditation means an official group checked the program's quality.

check.q: A school says you must sign a big loan today to keep your spot. What would you do?
options: Sign so you do not lose the spot
Sign but plan not to pay
Treat it as a red flag and take time to check
Ask AI to sign for you
check.why: Pressure to sign a big loan right away is a red flag.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Using AI as a study tutor
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask AI to explain, give examples and quiz you, without doing your work for you.
This lesson builds toward: Given a topic from your goal, you will ask an AI assistant to explain it, give an example and quiz you, without having AI do your assignments, and checking mistakes with your teacher or textbook.
An AI assistant can be a patient tutor, any time of day. Ask it to explain a topic simply, give an example, and quiz you: "I am studying fractions for my high school equivalency test. Explain how to add fractions in simple steps, give me one example, then give me three practice problems one at a time."
If you do not understand, say so: "Explain it a different way." "Use money as an example." The more you try problems yourself, the more you learn.
Do not have AI write your assignments or take your tests. Schools treat that as cheating, and you miss the learning. Also check facts: AI can make mistakes, even in math. Your textbook and teacher are the final word.
Step by step:
- Say what you are studying and your level.
- Ask for a simple explanation and one example.
- Ask for practice problems one at a time.
- Ask for a different explanation if stuck.
- Do your own assignments; check facts with your teacher or book.
Words to know:
- Tutor: a teacher who helps one person learn at their own pace.
- Academic honesty: doing your own work and following your school's rules.
Try it now: Pick one topic from your goal. Ask an AI assistant to explain it simply, give one example and quiz you with three questions one at a time.
You can now use AI as a study tutor in an honest way.

check.q: What should a good tutoring prompt include?
options: Only the word "help"
Your assignment so AI can finish it
Your student ID number
What you are studying and your level
check.why: Telling AI the topic and your level gets explanations that fit you.

check.q: You have an essay due and are tempted to let AI write it. What would you do?
options: Let AI write it and hand it in
Ask AI to explain the topic and quiz you, then write it yourself
Copy a classmate's essay
Skip the assignment
check.why: Having AI write assignments breaks school rules and skips the learning.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making a study plan that fits your life
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a weekly study plan around work and other commitments.
This lesson builds toward: Given your work and appointments, you will make a four-week study plan with AI help, with short, regular sessions and the first two in your calendar.
When you are working, attending appointments and caring for family, study time has to be planned. Short, regular sessions work better than cramming.
Ask AI: "I work 7 am to 3:30 pm on weekdays and have appointments on Tuesday afternoons. Make a four-week study plan for my high school equivalency math, with 30-minute sessions four times a week and a short review each weekend."
Put the sessions in your phone's calendar with reminders. Study somewhere quiet, such as a library, and use free library Wi-Fi and computers if you need them. If you miss a session, do not give up; just do the next one.
Step by step:
- List your work hours and fixed appointments.
- Ask AI for a four-week plan with short sessions.
- Put sessions in your calendar with reminders.
- Find a quiet place to study.
- If you miss one, just do the next.
Words to know:
- Study session: a set time you spend learning.
- Cramming: trying to learn a lot at the last minute.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for a four-week study plan that fits your work and appointments. Put your first two sessions in your phone's calendar.
You can now make and keep a study plan that fits your life.

options: Studying a little every day
Taking notes in class
Learning a lot at the last minute
Asking a tutor for help
check.why: Cramming means trying to learn a lot right before a test.

check.q: You missed Tuesday's study session because of work. What would you do?
options: Just do the next session
Quit the plan
Study for six hours on Wednesday
Start the whole plan over
check.why: Missing one session is fine; getting back on track is what matters.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Getting ready to apply for financial aid
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find where to apply for federal student aid and list what to prepare.
This lesson builds toward: Using studentaid.gov, you will list where to apply for federal student aid and what to prepare, with three questions for a financial aid office and private details typed only on studentaid.gov.
For college and many career schools in the United States, the first step for financial aid is the FAFSA, the Free Application for Federal Student Aid. As the name says, it is free. Apply only at the official site, studentaid.gov; do not pay any website to fill it out.
Rules about criminal convictions and student aid have changed in recent years. Do not assume you cannot get aid. Check the current rules on studentaid.gov, or ask the school's financial aid office; they help students with these questions every day.
AI can help you understand terms ("What is a Pell Grant?" "What is the difference between a grant and a loan?") and make a list of questions for the financial aid office. Type your personal and tax information only on studentaid.gov, never into AI. Grants do not have to be repaid; loans do.
Step by step:
- Go only to studentaid.gov for the FAFSA; it is free.
- Check current rules on convictions there or with the school's financial aid office.
- Use AI to explain terms and plan questions.
- Type personal information only on the official site.
- Know the difference: grants are not repaid, loans are.
Words to know:
- FAFSA: the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, at studentaid.gov.
- Grant: money for school that usually does not have to be paid back.
- Financial aid office: the office at a school that helps students pay for it.
Official sources:
- Federal Student Aid: studentaid.gov
Try it now: Final task: write your job-linked learning goal, check one real program with the five questions, ask AI for a four-week study plan, let it teach and quiz you on the first topic, and put your first two sessions in your calendar. If the program is college or career school, add three questions for its financial aid office.
You can now plan, find, check and pay for continuing education, and study with AI as your tutor.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Job-linked goal The goal is vague or not tied to a job. One sentence naming the job and the training it needs. Notes whether the job needs a state license and where to check. Program checked No program, or fewer than five questions answered. One real program checked with all five questions, answered by the program. Answers about cost are in writing, and a second program was compared. AI as tutor AI did the work, or no quiz was done. AI explained the first topic, gave an example and quizzed the learner. The learner asked AI to explain a different way when stuck. Study plan in calendar No plan, or no sessions in the calendar. A four-week plan with short, regular sessions, and the first two sessions in the calendar. Sessions have reminders and fit around work and appointments. Financial aid questions Missing when the program is college or career school. Three questions for the financial aid office. Also notes where to fill out the FAFSA for free. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: Federal Aid for Students and Adults
Free Application for Federal Student Aid
First Approved Funding for School Admission
Financial Account for Student Assistance
check.why: FAFSA is the Free Application for Federal Student Aid.

check.q: A website asks for a fee to fill out your FAFSA. What would you do?
options: Pay it to save time
Give them your tax details
Ask AI to fill it out with your Social Security number
Fill it out free on studentaid.gov
check.why: The FAFSA is free on studentaid.gov, and private details go only there.
